query: Equiatomic HfNbTaTiZr has 8–16% room-temperature tensile ductility in the cast state and a yield strength of 163–530 MPa at 1000 °C at strain rates of 10−4–10−2 s−1, but its poor oxygen resistance limits practical high-temperature use. What single intervention could overcome this limitation without sacrificing the alloy’s useful mechanical performance? Formulate one hypothesis specifying the intervention and mechanism, the predicted change relative to untreated cast HfNbTaTiZr, the relevant temperature, atmosphere, exposure time, and mechanical-loading boundaries, supporting prior evidence, and a controlled falsification experiment.

generation.hypothesis: A minor Al addition (on the order of a few atomic percent) to as-cast HfNbTaTiZr will form a stable alumina (Al2O3) scale during high-temperature exposure, thereby improving oxygen resistance without significantly degrading the alloy’s high-temperature strength or room-temperature ductility.
generation.material_initial_state: Equiatomic HfNbTaTiZr in as-cast form (8–16% RT ductility, 163–530 MPa yield strength at 1000 °C, strain rates of 10⁻⁴–10⁻² s⁻¹).
generation.intervention: Arc or induction melting under vacuum to incorporate a controlled minor fraction of Al (e.g., ~2–5 at%), followed by standard casting into molds.
generation.conditions: Exposure in air (or oxygen-rich environment) at 1000 °C for up to 100 h under moderate mechanical loading (strain rates of 10⁻⁴–10⁻² s⁻¹).
generation.structural_mediator: The formation of a continuous protective Al2O3 layer on the alloy surface.
generation.mechanism: Al in the alloy promotes a stable alumina film that acts as a barrier to oxygen diffusion, thereby mitigating its detrimental ingress and preserving the alloy’s mechanical performance.
generation.predicted_outcome: Significantly reduced oxidation mass gain compared to undoped HfNbTaTiZr, while retaining at least ~80–90% of the original yield strength and ductility under the specified temperature and strain-rate conditions.
generation.baseline: Undoped equiatomic HfNbTaTiZr alloy with poor oxygen resistance leading to performance losses at high temperatures.
generation.boundary: Applicable up to ~1000 °C in air for extended durations (≥100 h) under strain rates of 10⁻⁴–10⁻² s⁻¹. Higher Al additions or more extreme conditions may alter phase stability and microstructure.
generation.uncertainty: Exact optimal Al content and processing conditions need to be established experimentally to avoid unwanted phase transformations or loss of ductility.

falsification_experiment.design: Melt and cast nominal HfNbTaTiZr ingots both with and without ~2–5 at% Al addition. Expose specimens to air at 1000 °C for up to 100 h. Measure any mass gain, oxide-scale thickness, and record microstructural changes. Then perform room-temperature and high-temperature tensile tests on both sets of samples to compare ductility and yield strength.
measurements: Oxide-layer thickness and composition (e.g., via SEM/EDX, XRD)
Tensile properties (yield strength, ultimate strength, elongation to fracture) at RT and 1000 °C
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If oxidized Al-doped samples do not develop a continuous alumina scale and do not exhibit improved oxidation resistance or if mechanical properties degrade significantly below those of undoped HfNbTaTiZr, the hypothesis is falsified.

After discussing the law of strength change with temperature and analyzing the results of the transmission electron microscopy, it is concluded that the deformation of the alloy at high temperature is mainly controlled by dislocation, and the morphology and density of the dislocation control the mechanical properties of the alloy. We have not discussed the plasticity change before, so the next focus is to analyze the change in alloy plasticity at high temperature and the reasons for that change. The equiatomic HfMoNbTaTiZr alloy was chosen to analyze the effect of each constituent elemental by the subtraction method and, thus, HfMoNbTaTiZr, HfNbTaTiZr, HfMoTaTiZr, HfMoNbTiZr, HfMoNbTaZr, and HfMoNbTaTi were studied. Among these alloys, HfMoNbTaTi has the best mechanical performance, that is, 27% compressive strain at room temperature and yield strength 367 MPa at 1400 °C. HfMoNbTaTi has great potential for elevated-temperature applications. As the alloy system does not contain very expensive elements such as Re and Ru, it is cost competitive for high-temperature applications like Nb-Hf-Ti alloys in space vehicles. Further modification of composition and/or anti-oxidation coatings are still required for high-temperature applications in the air. According to the experiment results, the effects of Mo, Nb, Ta, Ti, and Zr on mechanical properties of equiatomic Hf-Mo-Nb-Ta-Ti-Zr alloys were described. For higher room-temperature strength, one should add an element which interacts frequently with the alloy, such as Mo. chosen.lever: minor Al addition to form a stable protective alumina scale
chosen.technique: arc or induction melting with controlled Al doping, followed by high-temperature exposure tests
chosen.conditions: high-temperature (up to 1000°C) exposure in air for extended durations under moderate mechanical loading
chosen.why: By introducing a small content of Al, the alloy can form a continuous Al2O3 layer at high temperatures, which slows oxygen ingress and mitigates its detrimental effects. Previous studies on refractory high-entropy alloys show that alumina scales provide effective oxidation resistance while maintaining mechanical strength. A controlled falsification experiment would compare microstructure, mass gain, oxide-layer integrity, and retention of mechanical properties between Al-doped and undoped samples subjected to the same high-temperature oxidation and loading conditions.
